crime.value: Stabbing murder of Karen Burson with a kitchen knife in her Brooklyn apartment; central question: how could the killer have let Burson in and then vanished from a building with no hiding places or exits?
crime.quote: "Homicide," Malliner said, staring intently. "She was stabbed, with a kitchen knife."

victim.value: Karen Burson, estranged wife who vindictively refused her husband a divorce and provoked hysterical scenes with men — likely including a lover in the building
victim.quote: "She told everybody," he said, "that she'd never give you a divorce. So there's your motive."

closed_world.value: Karen's ten-apartment Brooklyn walk-up: five tenants away, the rest alibied; fire escape wet-painted, skylight ladder jammed and dust-covered
closed_world.quote: "Ten apartments," Malliner said. "Five of them empty, tenants were in the country for the weekend and can prove it."

culprit_and_motive.value: Richard Rayburn, fourth-floor tenant and presumed lover, killed Karen (driven to it by her hysterical goading) and framed Burson by swapping name plates
culprit_and_motive.quote: "Rayburn killed her before I came, and later on that night he put the name-plates back the way they belonged"

resolution.value: During the forced reenactment Burson realizes the doorbell name plates had been switched; he announces Rayburn's fingerprints will be on the backs of the cards, Rayburn bolts and is seized, and the inspector rebukes Malliner
resolution.quote: "Rayburn's fingerprints are on the back of the two name cards. On the backs—"

investigator.value: Clyde Burson, the accused suspect himself, solving the crime under interrogation; police Lt. Malliner and Det. Perinsky serve as antagonistic official investigators
investigator.quote: "Find out who really killed her," he said in a tight voice. "You have the wrong man."

suspect_architecture.value: Closed-building cast: Burson, the estranged husband with motive (wife refused divorce), opportunity (was in the apartment) and physical evidence against him; the building's ten apartments systematically eliminated — five empty, an 85-year-old woman too frail, two couples with company, a girl with her boyfriend — leaving Rayburn, the red-headed tenant, who is the actual killer but appears exonerated as an eyewitness against Burson.
suspect_architecture.quote: "Ten apartments," Malliner said. "Five of them empty... finally there's this guy Rayburn, who saw you."

red_herring.value: The overwhelming physical trace evidence against Burson — fingerprints on the bureau, blood on his shoes, jacket threads on the desk, the ransacked desk — all genuine but innocently produced, plus the false movie alibi that discredits him; also Burson's speculation about a hidden killer escaping via skylight or fire escape.
red_herring.quote: Fingerprints, with blown-up photographs... Traces of blood on the shoes he'd worn yesterday. Threads from his jacket

clue_fairness.value: Fair: the reader is given the vestibule name-plate detail early — Burson's visiting card with 'Mrs.' in red ink, and his memory of ringing 'the second bell from the end' — before the reconstruction shows that bell now belongs to the old lady, and the old lady's denial is shown to the reader in scene.
clue_fairness.quote: "she was still using one of my visiting cards and she'd written Mrs. in front of my name, in red ink."

social_world.value: Brooklyn precinct-house power politics: a lieutenant racing to close a case before Homicide or 'the big brass' learn of it, using good-cop/bad-cop pressure on a lone civilian; Inspector O'Shea's arrival represents the higher authority that ultimately checks Malliner's careerism.
social_world.quote: "We'll have it all wrapped up before homicide or the big brass know what we're doing."

alibi.value: Burson's false alibi — a Radio City movie from three to six — collapses immediately against two eyewitnesses; Rayburn's genuine-seeming alibi is that he was on the stoop with the janitress when Burson rang, which conceals that he had already killed Karen and switched the name plates.
alibi.quote: "I went to a movie at Radio City. I had to wait on line quite awhile."

reveal_mechanic.value: Physical reenactment in the vestibule: Burson presses the second bell from the end and it is the old lady's, proving the name plates were switched on the day of the murder; the demonstrable proof is Rayburn's fingerprints on the backs of the two name cards, and Rayburn's flight confirms it.
reveal_mechanic.quote: "Rayburn's fingerprints are on the back of the two name cards. On the backs—"

media_and_audience.value: Perception is managed inside the police institution rather than by press: Malliner packages Burson as the obvious guilty man ('there's your motive... I wish every case was as easy as this one'), and neighbours' impressions — that Burson looked drunk and green in the face — shape the public account of the crime.
media_and_audience.quote: "She told everybody," he said, "that she'd never give you a divorce. So there's your motive."

investigator_wound.value: Burson, the accused who must investigate his own case, is undone by his own belief in truth and justice and his exhaustion; Malliner's wound is a personal grudge and hatred of killers that blinds him to alternatives, plus ambition to close the case first.
investigator_wound.quote: Malliner, who went at Burson with the single-minded malice of a deep grudge. No reason for it.

victims_enemies.value: Karen Burson antagonized the men in her life: her estranged husband Clyde, whom she refused a divorce and taunted with 'you want to kill me' scenes, and a presumed lover — tenant Richard Rayburn — whom she likely goaded into the same frenzy.
victims_enemies.quote: “Kill me—that’s what you want—go ahead and do it!”

suspect_wounds.value: Burson's wound is his belief in truth and justice combined with his fatal instinct to lie: he loves Elise and wants a divorce, so he panicked at the body, ransacked the desk, wiped prints, and lied about the movie — every self-protective act deepened his guilt.
suspect_wounds.quote: He wasn’t even a good liar; he believed in truth and justice and the good will of men.

unreliable_frame.value: The story is told through Burson's guarded interior monologue: he lies openly to police while the reader sees the truth, so his 'innocent' account is compromised; Malliner's confident reconstruction is equally untrustworthy, and Rayburn's eyewitness testimony is self-serving fabrication.
unreliable_frame.quote: You weren’t there, he told himself. Remember that, and stick to it. They can’t prove otherwise.

setting_as_constraint.value: A Brooklyn walk-up apartment house: entry requires ringing a name-plate bell so a tenant can buzz you in; ten apartments all accounted for, wet paint on the fire escape and undisturbed dust on the skylight ladder seal every exit — Rayburn exploited the bell/name-plate system as his alibi machine.
setting_as_constraint.quote: “The fire escape had wet paint, and nobody went down it. And the ladder to the skylight was jammed.”

evidence_type.value: Physical/forensic — latent fingerprints on the reverse of the switched vestibule name cards, the trace left by Rayburn handling and restoring the plates.
evidence_type.quote: “Rayburn’s fingerprints are on the back of the two name cards. On the backs—”

false_suspect.value: Clyde Burson, the estranged husband — fingerprints, blood-traced shoes, jacket threads on the desk, a girlfriend, a refused divorce, and two eyewitnesses; framed both by circumstance and by Rayburn's arrangement.
false_suspect.quote: Malliner had his fall guy; he had Clyde Burson.

technical_detail.value: The vestibule buzzer/name-plate mechanism: by swapping Karen's card with old Mrs. Henshaw's (3A), Rayburn made the already-dead Karen appear to answer her bell — Burson actually rang the old lady's bell, second from the end, and she buzzed him in.
technical_detail.quote: “he switched the name plates downstairs, Karen’s and the little old lady’s”

moral_ambiguity.value: Rayburn is implicitly a man Karen drove to murder with her hysterical goading, as she once nearly drove her husband; and Malliner's railroading is not corruption but ambition and a hatred of killers — he genuinely believes the evidence.
moral_ambiguity.quote: he was certain she’d had a lover, and must have whipped him into a frenzy and screamed at him the same way
